metastasis. A retrospective analysis conducted in the cytokine era indicated that patients most likely to benefit from cytoreductive nephrectomy before 
systemic therapy were those with lung-only metastases, good prognostic features, and good performance status.116 Retrospective data from the IMDC 
suggested that cytoreductive nephrectomy continues to play a role in patients treated with VEGF-targeted agents.117 The efficacy of newer systemic 
therapies is challenging the standard in some patients with metastatic disease. Results from the CARMENA phase III trial of patients with metastatic 
RCC who were eligible for cytoreductive nephrectomy found that sunitinib alone was non-inferior to sunitinib after nephrectomy.118 The median OS was 
18.4 months in the sunitinib-alone group and 13.9 months in the sunitinib after nephrectomy group (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.71–1.10), which did not exceed 
the fixed non-inferiority limit (1.20). However, many of the patients in this trial had poor-risk features, underscoring the importance of patient selection to 
obtain the greatest benefit from nephrectomy or targeted therapy.118,119 A post-hoc analysis of the CARMENA trial reported that for patients with only one 
IMDC risk factor, OS was longer following nephrectomy (31.4 months vs. 25.2 months).120 At this point, there are no prospective data defining the role of 
cytoreductive nephrectomy in patients who subsequently receive checkpoint antibody therapy. However, the ongoing open-label, randomized, 
prospective SEVURO-CN trial is investigating initial cytoreductive nephrectomy prior to IO-based therapy, as well as deferred cytoreductive 
nephrectomy, compared to IO therapy only in patients with synchronous metastatic RCC (Clinical Trial ID: NCT05753839). Further study will better 
define the role and timing of cytoreductive nephrectomy in the rapidly evolving treatment landscape for RCC. There are two ongoing randomized phase 
III trials investigating deferred cytoreductive nephrectomy following immuno-oncology (IO)-based therapy in patients with synchronous metastatic RCC: 
the PROBE (SWOG 1931) trial (Clinical Trial ID: NCT04510597) and the NORDIC-SUN trial (Clinical Trial ID: NCT03977571). 

Besides cytoreductive nephrectomy, the Panel also recommends upfront systemic therapy for patients with stage IV, M1 potentially resectable primary 
disease and large-volume distant metastases or large sarcomatoid tumors over initial cytoreductive nephrectomy. For these patients, clinical trial is also 
an option (category 2B). In patients whose tumors are surgically unresectable (stage IV T4,M0 or M1), the Panel recommends performing tissue 
sampling to confirm diagnosis of RCC to determine histology and guide subsequent management. Systemic therapy is generally recommended after 

MS-15

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
recurrence, after cytoreductive nephrectomy in patients with multiple metastatic sites, or for patients with surgically unresectable tumors. See Systemic 
Therapy Options for Patients with Relapsed or Stage IV Disease below for detailed recommendations. 

Patients with metastatic disease who present with hematuria or other symptoms related to the primary tumor should be offered palliative nephrectomy if 
they are surgical candidates. In addition, the small subset of patients with potentially surgically resectable primary RCC and oligometastatic sites are 
candidates for nephrectomy and management of metastases by surgical metastasectomy; alternatively, SBRT or percutaneous ablation are available for 
selected patients as well. Candidates include patients who: 1) initially present with primary RCC and oligometastatic sites; or 2) develop oligometastases 
after a prolonged disease-free interval from nephrectomy. Oligometastatic sites that are amenable to this approach include the lung, bone, and brain. 
The primary tumor and the metastases may be resected during the same operation or at different times. Most patients who undergo targeted treatment 
of oligometastases experience recurrence, but long-term relapse-free survival has been reported in these patients. Prospective phase II studies showed 
some patients may benefit from SBRT treatment for oligometastases, postponing time to systemic therapy.121-123 SBRT may offer durable local control for 
metastases.124 It should be considered for a patient with oligometastases unless metastasectomy is planned or SBRT cannot be delivered due to 
anatomic site, proximity to organs at risk, or previous treatment.121-126 For detailed recommendations on normal tissue constraints, as well as SBRT 
dosing and fractionation for distant metastatic disease, see Principles of Radiation Therapy in the Guidelines. 

Patients who have undergone a nephrectomy and years later develop an oligometastatic recurrence also have the option of metastasectomy, SBRT,127-

129 or percutaneous ablation, in addition to the first-line therapy options below. Clinical trial is an option for all patients, regardless of histology. Best 
supportive care is also recommended for all patients in this setting (see the Supportive Care section later in this Discussion). 

Systemic Therapy Options for Patients with Relapsed or Stage IV Disease 

Targeted therapy utilizing TKIs, and/or anti-VEGF antibodies, has been widely used in first- and second-line treatments. Agents targeting the mammalian 
target of rapamycin (mTOR) are also used in highly selected settings. A number of targeted agents have been approved by the FDA for the treatment of 
advanced RCC in the first and/or subsequent lines of therapy. ICIs provided a revolution in treatment options. Checkpoint antibodies alter the interaction 
between immune cells and antigen-presenting cells, including tumor cells. These agents can augment an anti-tumor immune response and have shown 
promise in a number of tumor indications. 

Tumor histology and risk stratification of patients are important in therapy selection. The NCCN Guidelines for Kidney Cancer stratify treatment 
recommendations by histology. Recommendations for first-line treatment of ccRCC are also stratified by risk group based on the MSKCC Prognostic 
Model and the IMDC prognostic criteria. 

NCCN Categories of Preference 
To further guide management of advanced RCC, the NCCN Kidney Cancer Panel has categorized all systemic kidney cancer therapy regimens as 
“Preferred,” “Other Recommended,” or “Useful in Certain Circumstances.” This categorization provides guidance on treatment selection by considering 

MS-16

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
the efficacy, safety, evidence, and other factors that play a role in treatment selection. These factors include pre-existing comorbidities, nature of the 
disease, and in some cases consideration of access to agents. 

Data Tables According to Line of Treatment and RCC Histology (Key Studies) 
Due to the increasing number of NCCN-recommended systemic therapy options for metastatic RCC, the Panel has organized efficacy data from key 
studies into tables according to RCC histology and line of treatment (when applicable) for category 1 and 2A, preferred, and other recommended 
regimens; see Table 1, Table 2, and Table 3 at the end of this Discussion. 

Information about drug mechanism of action, FDA approval, summaries of study conclusions and safety data, and Categories of Evidence and 
Consensus and Categories of Preference for NCCN-recommended regimens remains below, and is stratified by RCC histology, line of treatment (when 
applicable), prior IO therapy status (when applicable), and Categories of Preference. 

First-Line Systemic Therapy Options for Patients with Stage IV (M1 or Unresectable T4,M0) or Relapsed Clear Cell RCC 

Preferred 

Axitinib + Pembrolizumab (All Risk Groups) 
Axitinib is a selective, second-generation TKI of VEGFRs, while pembrolizumab is a monoclonal antibody that selectively binds to PD-1 (expressed on 
activated T cells) and blocks the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2 (both expressed on tumor cells and antigen-presenting 
cells). In April 2019, the FDA approved axitinib in combination with pembrolizumab for first-line treatment of patients with advanced RCC. Data from the 
randomized phase III KEYNOTE-426 trial, which included patients with favorable-, intermediate-, or poor-risk RCC, supported the combination therapy’s 
approval for this indication. Patients received either axitinib + pembrolizumab or sunitinib; those receiving the combination regimen had a significantly 
higher overall response rate (ORR) and longer PFS than those receiving sunitinib.130 Subsequent analyses at 31-, 43-, and 67-month median follow-ups 
showed agreement with these data (see Table 1 for most recent efficacy data).131-133 Median OS in the most recent follow-up (median 67.2 months) was 
longer in the axitinib + pembrolizumab arm compared to the sunitinib arm.133 Frequent AEs of grade 3 or higher in the axitinib + pembrolizumab arm 
included hypertension, diarrhea, and elevated alanine aminotransferase.131 Based on these data, the Panel recommends first-line axitinib + 
pembrolizumab as a category 1, preferred option for patients with ccRCC across all risk groups. 

Cabozantinib + Nivolumab (All Risk Groups) 
Cabozantinib is a multitargeted TKI of VEGFRs, MET, and AXL, while nivolumab is an anti–PD-1 antibody. In January 2021, the FDA approved 
cabozantinib in combination with nivolumab for first-line treatment of patients with advanced RCC. Data from the randomized phase III CheckMate 9ER 
trial, which included patients with favorable-, intermediate-, or poor-risk RCC, supported the combination therapy’s approval for this indication. Patients 
received either cabozantinib + nivolumab or sunitinib monotherapy. Those receiving cabozantinib + nivolumab had significantly higher ORRs and longer 
PFS than those receiving sunitinib. Additionally, OS was significantly longer with cabozantinib + nivolumab than sunitinib, and the HR favored 

MS-17

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
cabozantinib + nivolumab (HR for death, 0.60; 98.89% CI, 0.40–0.89; P = .001).134 In a subgroup analysis, the cabozantinib + nivolumab arm showed 
improved PFS, OS, and ORR in patients with advanced RCC with sarcomatoid features (an aggressive histologic subtype associated with poor 
prognosis) when compared to sunitinib.135 Patients receiving combination treatment also reported delayed time to deterioration of patient-reported 
outcome scores compared to sunitinib.136 Frequent AEs of grade 3 or 4 included hypertension, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, and diarrhea.135 In the 
final analysis at median follow-up of 67.6 months, the cabozantinib + nivolumab combination continued to show clinically meaningful benefit over 
sunitinib, with longer OS and PFS and higher ORR (see Table 1 for recent efficacy data).137 Based on these data, the Panel recommends first-line 
cabozantinib + nivolumab as a category 1, preferred option for patients with ccRCC across all risk groups. 

Ipilimumab + Nivolumab (All Risk Groups) 
Ipilimumab is a monoclonal antibody that selectively blocks the interaction between the negative regulator cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4; 
expressed early on activated T cells) and its ligands CD80/CD86 (expressed on antigen-presenting cells). Nivolumab’s mechanism of action was 
described previously. In April 2018, the FDA approved ipilimumab in combination with nivolumab for first-line treatment of patients with poor-
/intermediate-risk advanced RCC. Data from the randomized phase III CheckMate 214 trial, which supported the FDA approval, compared combination 
ipilimumab + nivolumab followed by nivolumab monotherapy with sunitinib monotherapy in patients with advanced RCC.138 The study’s coprimary 
endpoints were ORR, OS, and PFS in patients with intermediate- and poor-risk RCC only; exploratory analyses of data in patients with favorable-risk 
RCC were reported separately. In patients with intermediate-/poor-risk RCC, combination ipilimumab + nivolumab led to a higher ORR and CR rate 
versus sunitinib monotherapy. Updated analyses continued to show a combined OS and ORR for intermediate-/poor-risk RCC that favored ipilimumab + 
nivolumab over sunitinib. In the primary analysis for patients with intermediate-/poor-risk RCC, longer OS was reported with ipilimumab + nivolumab 
versus sunitinib; however, PFS was not statistically significant per the predetermined threshold (HR for disease progression or death, 0.82; 99.1% CI, 
0.64–1.05; P = 0.03).138 Longer follow-up suggested improved PFS, with an HR of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.62–0.85).139,140 

In initial analyses, OS benefit for patients with favorable-risk RCC with ipilimumab + nivolumab was not observed (HR, 1.45 at 25-month follow-up);138 
however, a trend towards improved OS in the combination was observed in an exploratory analysis of this patient population at the 8-year follow-up (HR, 
0.82; 95% CI, 0.60–1.13).140 Updated efficacy data for all risk groups are found in Table 1. Treatment-related AEs occurred in 93% of patients in the 
ipilimumab + nivolumab group and 97% of patients in the sunitinib group; grade 3 or 4 events occurred in 46% and 63% of patients, respectively. AEs led 
to treatment discontinuation in 22% and 12% of patients receiving ipilimumab + nivolumab and sunitinib, respectively. Treatment-related deaths occurred 
in 8 patients receiving combination therapy and 4 patients receiving sunitinib. Thirty-five percent of patients who developed immune-mediated AEs after 
ipilimumab + nivolumab treatment received high-dose steroids.138 Based on these data, the Panel recommends first-line ipilimumab + nivolumab as a 
category 1, preferred treatment option for patients with ccRCC across risk groups. 

MS-18

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
Lenvatinib + Pembrolizumab (All Risk Groups) 
Lenvatinib is a multitargeted TKI of VEGFR-1, -2, and -3; fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR)-1, -2, -3, and 4; platelet-derived growth factor 
receptor-α (PDGFR-α); c-KIT; and RET. Pembrolizumab’s mechanism of action was described previously. In August 2021, the FDA approved lenvatinib 
in combination with pembrolizumab for first-line treatment of patients with advanced RCC. Data from the randomized phase III CLEAR trial, which 
included patients with favorable-, intermediate-, or poor-risk RCC, supported the combination therapy’s approval for this indication. Patients received 
either lenvatinib + pembrolizumab, everolimus/lenvatinib, or sunitinib. Those receiving lenvatinib + pembrolizumab had significantly longer PFS and a 
higher ORR than those receiving sunitinib, which were maintained in follow-up analyses.141-143 At median 49-month follow-up, OS was favorable for 
lenvatinib + pembrolizumab compared to sunitinib (see Table 1 for most recent efficacy data).143 In contrast, OS was not significantly different between 
the everolimus/lenvatinib and sunitinib groups.141 The final analysis noted that ~85% of patients treated with lenvatinib + pembrolizumab had treatment-
emergent AEs (grade 3 or higher), which included hypertension and diarrhea, versus ~75% of patients who received sunitinib, consistent with prior safety 
profile analyses.143 Based on these data, the Panel recommends first-line lenvatinib + pembrolizumab as a category 1, preferred treatment option for 
patients with ccRCC across all risk groups. 

Cabozantinib (Poor-/Intermediate-Risk Groups) 
In the open-label, randomized, phase II CABOSUN trial, patients with intermediate- or poor-risk advanced RCC received either cabozantinib or 
sunitinib.144 See Table 1 for efficacy data. Those treated with cabozantinib showed a significantly increased PFS and higher ORR compared to those 
treated with sunitinib. The percentage of patients who experienced AEs of any grade or grade 3 or 4 was similar between cabozantinib and sunitinib. 
The most frequently reported AEs with cabozantinib included diarrhea, hypertension, fatigue, and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia.144 Cabozantinib 
also increased quality-adjusted time without symptoms of disease or toxicity (Q-TWiST) versus sunitinib (317 days vs. 180 days, respectfully, with no 
disease progression and no grade 3 or 4 AEs).145 

Based on these results, the Panel recommends first-line cabozantinib as a category 2A, preferred treatment option for patients with poor- and 
intermediate-risk ccRCC. 

Other Recommended 

Axitinib + Avelumab (All Risk Groups) 
Avelumab is a monoclonal antibody that selectively binds to PD-L1; axitinib’s mechanism of action was described previously. In May 2019, the FDA 
approved axitinib + avelumab for first-line treatment of patients with advanced RCC. Data from the randomized phase III JAVELIN Renal 101 trial, which 
included patients with favorable-, intermediate-, or poor-risk RCC, supported the combination therapy’s approval for this indication.146,147 For both the 
overall population and PD-L1–positive patients, those receiving axitinib + avelumab had significantly longer PFS than those receiving sunitinib. This 
benefit was observed across all risk groups. For OS, data were immature for all groups in both the primary146 and 13-month interim147 analyses. In the 
final analysis at an approximate median of 74 months, median OS was ~45 months with axitinib + avelumab versus ~39 months with sunitinib in the 

MS-19

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
overall population but was not statistically significant (see Table 1).148 PFS was significantly longer and ORR was higher with the combination versus 
sunitinib.148,149 Incidence of AEs of any grade, or grade 3 or higher, was similar between treatment arms,146 and no new safety signals were reported in 
the extended follow-up.148,149 Based on these results, the Panel recommends first-line axitinib + avelumab as a category 2A, other recommended 
treatment option for patients with ccRCC across all risk groups. 

The post-hoc analysis of 108 patients with sarcomatoid histology in the phase III JAVELIN Renal 101 trial showed that patients in the avelumab + axitinib 
treatment arm had improved PFS (stratified HR, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.325–1.003) and a higher ORR (46.8% vs. 21.3%; complete response [CR] in 4.3% vs. 
0%) versus those in the sunitinib arm.150 

Pazopanib (All Risk Groups) 
Pazopanib is an oral multitargeted TKI/angiogenesis inhibitor of VEGFRs, PDGFR-α and -β, and c-KIT, ITK, LCK, and c-FMS. The drug’s safety and 
efficacy were evaluated in an open-label phase III study. Patients with advanced ccRCC who received 0–1 prior treatment received either pazopanib or 
placebo (see Table 1 for efficacy data). PFS was significantly longer and ORR was significantly higher with pazopanib versus placebo in the treatment-
naïve sub-population,151 but there was no difference in OS between the two groups.152 Notable grade 3 toxicity was hepatotoxicity, indicated by elevated 
levels of alanine (30%) and aspartate (21%) transaminases.151 Therefore, it is critical to monitor liver function before and during treatment with the drug. 

Additionally, the COMPARZ non-inferiority study of sunitinib versus pazopanib showed that these two drugs have similar safety and efficacy (see Table 1 
for efficacy data).153,154 Based on these data, the Panel has listed first-line pazopanib as a category 2A, other recommended regimen for patients with 
ccRCC across all risk groups. 

Sunitinib (All Risk Groups) 
Sunitinib is a multikinase inhibitor targeting several receptor tyrosine kinases, including PDGFR-α and -β; VEGFR-1, -2, and -3; c-KIT; FLT3; CSF-1R; 
and RET.155-158 The efficacy of first-line sunitinib was studied in a randomized phase III trial in which patients with metastatic RCC received either 
sunitinib or IFN-α.155 See Table 1 for efficacy data. PFS was longer in those receiving sunitinib across all risk groups. Updated results demonstrated a 
strong trend towards OS advantage of sunitinib over IFN-α in the first-line setting.159 Based on these data, the Panel includes first-line sunitinib as a 
category 2A, other recommended regimen for patients with ccRCC across all risk groups. 

Cabozantinib (Favorable-Risk Group) 
Extrapolating on the CABOSUN data for patients with poor-/intermediate-risk (see above), the Panel added first-line cabozantinib as a category 2B, other 
recommended regimen for patients with favorable-risk ccRCC. 

MS-20

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
Useful in Certain Circumstances 

Active Surveillance for Select, Asymptomatic Patients with ccRCC 
A subset of patients with advanced ccRCC show indolent progression of disease and could benefit from initial active surveillance because of the toxicity 
of systemic therapies. A phase II trial of patients with treatment-naïve, asymptomatic, metastatic RCC followed patients on active surveillance through 
radiographic assessment at defined intervals until a decision was made to initiate systemic therapy.160 Of the 48 patients included in the analysis, the 
median time of surveillance from registration to initiation of systemic therapy was 14.9 months. This study demonstrated that a subset of patients with 
advanced ccRCC can safely undergo active surveillance before starting systemic therapy. In a prospective observational study of 504 patients with 
metastatic RCC, the median OS was not reached (95% CI, 122 months to not estimable [NE]) in patients who received active surveillance versus 30 
months for those treated with systemic therapy.161,162 Therefore, the Panel included active surveillance as a category 2A, useful in certain circumstances 
option for select, asymptomatic patients with favorable-risk ccRCC. 

Axitinib (All Risk Groups) 
As a second-line therapy for patients with ccRCC, axitinib treatment led to higher ORR and longer median PFS compared with sorafenib.163 In a 
randomized phase III trial, treatment-naïve patients received either axitinib or sorafenib; PFS was not significantly longer in patients receiving axitinib 
versus sorafenib but had an acceptable toxicity profile.164 Based on these data, the Panel has included first-line axitinib as a category 2B, useful in 
certain circumstances option for patients with ccRCC across all risk groups. 

Subsequent Systemic Therapy Options for Patients with Clear Cell RCC 

The NCCN Kidney Cancer Panel stratified the subsequent therapies for ccRCC based on whether the patients have received any prior IO therapy. The 
recommended options are categorized into “IO therapy naïve” and “prior IO therapy.” Certain regimens (ie, axitinib, cabozantinib, nivolumab, tivozanib) 
are category 2A options in this setting because of the Panel’s observation that randomized registrational trials for these monotherapies began prior to the 
approval of IO combination therapy, and very few patients enrolled on these trials received upfront IO combination therapy. Therefore, the data do not 
support category 1 level evidence for subsequent monotherapy after frontline TKIs in the era of IO combination therapy, despite the limited number of 
phase III trials for IO combinations in this setting. 

Additionally, IO/TKI combinations for those who received prior IO therapy are designated as category 2B recommendations in this setting. Data to 
support the use of IO therapy following progression on IO therapy are lacking. Two randomized phase III trials investigating the use of IO/TKI 
combinations suggest IO therapy not be considered for patients who previously received it. In the CONTACT-03 trial, patients previously treated with IO 
with locally advanced or metastatic RCC were randomized to either atezolizumab (PD-L1 inhibitor) + cabozantinib or cabozantinib monotherapy.165 PFS 
was not statistically significant between treatment arms (HR, 1.03; P = .78), and HR for death was 0.94 (P = .69). Serious AEs were reported for 48% of 
patients treated with the combination compared to 33% treated with cabozantinib. Discontinuation of treatment due to AEs occurred in 16% of patients 
with the combination, compared to 4% with monotherapy.165 In the phase III TiNivo2 trial, patients with metastatic RCC who previously received IO 

MS-21

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
therapy were randomized to either tivozanib + nivolumab or tivozanib alone.166 Likewise, PFS was 5.7 months versus 7.4 months in the combination 
versus monotherapy arms, respectively (HR, 1.10; P = .49). The authors reported that this result was independent of where in the treatment sequence IO 
therapy was used.166 

Cabozantinib 
In the randomized phase III METEOR trial, patients with disease progression after previous TKI therapy received cabozantinib or everolimus. See Table 
2 for efficacy data. Median PFS was significantly longer and ORR significantly higher in patients receiving cabozantinib versus everolimus.167 The final 
analysis of the METEOR trial showed a statistically significant increase in OS in the cabozantinib arm versus the everolimus arm.168,169 Common grade 3 
or 4 AEs that occurred more frequently with cabozantinib than with everolimus included hypertension, diarrhea, fatigue, hypomagnesaemia, and palmar-
plantar erythrodysesthesia syndrome.167 Additionally, a network meta-analysis comparing the relative effectiveness of subsequent treatment options for 
advanced and metastatic ccRCC found cabozantinib offered greater PFS, OS, and ORR benefit over everolimus, lenvatinib monotherapy, nivolumab, 
pazopanib, axitinib, sorafenib, temsirolimus, and tivozanib, but not over everolimus/lenvatinib combination. The odds of severe AEs were improved with 
cabozantinib over everolimus/lenvatinib and lenvatinib monotherapy.170 Cabozantinib has also been used as the control arm for two studies that included 
patients who received prior IO therapy (CONTACT-03, described above, and the randomized CANTATA trial). CANTATA was a randomized trial 
investigating the addition of glutaminase inhibitor telaglenastat to cabozantinib.171 In both studies, there was no statistically significant survival difference 
between the experimental and control arms.165,171 

Based on these data, the Panel has included cabozantinib as a category 2A, other recommended subsequent therapy option for patients with ccRCC 
regardless of their prior IO therapy status. 

Everolimus/Lenvatinib 
In May 2016, the FDA approved lenvatinib, a multitargeted kinase inhibitor, in combination with everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, for treating advanced 
RCC following one prior anti-angiogenic therapy. In a randomized phase II trial, patients with metastatic or unresectable, locally advanced ccRCC who 
had received prior antiangiogenic therapy received either combination everolimus/lenvatinib, single-agent lenvatinib, or single-agent everolimus. See 
Table 2 for efficacy data. PFS and OS were significantly longer in patients receiving everolimus/lenvatinib versus everolimus monotherapy.172,173 Diarrhea 
was the most common grade 3 or 4 AE for those receiving everolimus/lenvatinib.172 A prospective study of 55 patients with metastatic ccRCC, heavily 
pretreated with prior ICIs and VEGFR-TKIs, showed a median PFS of 6.2 months and median OS of 12.2 months with everolimus/lenvatinib.174 Based on 
the phase II trial data, the Panel considers everolimus/lenvatinib a category 2A, other recommended subsequent therapy option for patients with ccRCC 
regardless of their prior IO therapy status. 

Nivolumab 
In the randomized phase III CheckMate 025 trial, patients with advanced ccRCC who were previously treated with one or more lines of anti-angiogenic 
therapy (excluding mTOR inhibitors) received either nivolumab or everolimus. See Table 2 for efficacy data. Patients receiving nivolumab had 

MS-22

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
significantly longer OS and significantly higher ORR than those receiving everolimus.175 The most prevalent grade 3 or 4 AEs with nivolumab were 
fatigue, anemia, and elevated levels of alanine and aspartate aminotransferases.176 Based on these data, the Panel has included nivolumab as a 
category 2A, subsequent therapy option for patients with ccRCC who have not received any prior IO therapy. 

Axitinib 
The randomized phase III AXIS study compared second-line axitinib versus sorafenib. See Table 2 for efficacy data. PFS was significantly longer and 
ORR significantly higher in patients receiving axitinib versus sorafenib.163 The most prevalent AEs of grade 3 or higher for those treated with axitinib 
included hypertension, diarrhea, and fatigue.177 Based on these data, the Panel included axitinib as a category 2A other recommended subsequent 
therapy option for patients with prior IO therapy and useful in certain circumstances for patients naïve for any prior IO therapy. 

Axitinib + Pembrolizumab 
Upon axitinib + pembrolizumab’s FDA approval in a first-line setting, the Panel discussed whether the combination therapy might be used in clinical 
practice as an off-label subsequent treatment option in patients with relapsed or stage IV ccRCC. While they conceded that there were no robust, 
published data to support the use of axitinib + pembrolizumab in a second-line setting, they thought that clinicians were likely to consider the combination 
as a treatment option in patients with advanced ccRCC whose disease progressed after first-line sunitinib therapy. A retrospective study on 38 patients 
with ccRCC who had disease progression and previously received either ICI or VEGFR-TKI therapy were administered axitinib + pembrolizumab.178 
Median PFS was 9.7 months (95% CI, 4.1–15.3) at a median follow-up of 17.1 months. The ORR was 25% (all partial responses [PRs]). Among 17 
patients who had previously received ipilimumab + nivolumab and then second-line axitinib + pembrolizumab, the median PFS was 11.1 months and 
ORR was 31.4%. About 87% of patients in this study experienced AEs associated with the combination regimen, and hypertension, fatigue, and diarrhea 
were the most prevalent.178 The Panel added axitinib + pembrolizumab as a category 2A, other recommended option for patients who are IO therapy 
naïve. This combination is useful in certain circumstances for patients with prior IO therapy (category 2B). 

Cabozantinib + Nivolumab 
Apolo et al 2020179 published data from an ongoing phase I dose escalation trial (ie, NCT02496208) in which patients with metastatic urothelial 
carcinoma or other genitourinary tumors (including three patients with ccRCC) received combination cabozantinib + nivolumab with or without 
ipilimumab; data from patients with ccRCC were not reported separately. A pooled analysis of the phase I dose-finding cohort and seven subsequent 
expansion cohorts, which included 16 patients with metastatic ccRCC, was reported.180 See Table 2 for efficacy data. In these patients, median OS was 
43.6 months (95% CI, 19.4–NE). Although there are no prospective or retrospective published data showing the benefit of cabozantinib + nivolumab in 
later lines of therapy in the treatment of advanced RCC, the Panel’s decision was based on available data for combined ICI/TKI combinations of similar 
class such as lenvatinib + pembrolizumab and axitinib + pembrolizumab. The Panel added cabozantinib + nivolumab as a category 2A, other 
recommended option for patients who are IO therapy naïve. This combination is useful in certain circumstances for patients with prior IO therapy 
(category 2B). 

MS-23

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
Ipilimumab + Nivolumab 
The phase I CheckMate 016 trial included treatment-naïve patients and those who had received one to four or more prior treatment regimens. Only the 
ORR results were stratified by treatment status: ORRs in the N3I1 and N1I3 were approximately 46% and 39%, respectively. OS and PFS data were not 
stratified by treatment line, but were similar.181 In a single-arm, phase II trial (TITAN-RCC), 32% of the 98 patients who had disease progression after 
second-line nivolumab had an objective response (OR) with ipilimumab/nivolumab. AEs of any grade occurred in 83% of patients, with grade 3 or 4 AEs 
occurring in 40% of patients.182 In the randomized phase II FRACTION-RCC trial, patients whose disease progressed on or after IO therapy had an ORR 
of 17.4% on ipilimumab/nivolumab and median duration of response (DOR) of 16.4 months (see Table 2). Similarly to TITAN-RCC, AEs of any grade 
occurred in 78% of patients, with AEs of grade 3 or 4 occurring in 28%.183 Two of the most common AEs of grade 3 or 4 reported in both trials were 
elevated lipase and diarrhea.182,183 Based on these data, the Panel considers ipilimumab + nivolumab as a category 2A, other recommended option for 
patients who are IO therapy naïve and useful in certain circumstances option for patients with prior IO therapy. 

Belzutifan 
Belzutifan inhibits the transcription factor hypoxia-inducible factor 2α (HIF-2α) and blocks the heterodimerization of HIF-2α with HIF-1β, thereby inducing 
tumor regression. Follow-up from an expansion cohort of patients, with ccRCC in a phase I/II trial of belzutifan, who had received 1 or more prior 
therapies showed a disease control rate of 80% among 55 patients. Median PFS was 14.5 months with 51% reporting PFS of 12 months. The most 
common AEs reported were anemia, fatigue, hypoxia, and dyspnea, among others.184 Based on these results, belzutifan was considered well tolerated 
with a favorable safety profile as a single agent. Belzutifan was approved by the FDA for patients with advanced RCC who were previously treated with a 
PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitor and VEGF-TKI. The open-label, randomized, phase III Litespark-005 trial compared belzutifan to everolimus in 746 patients with 
advanced ccRCC whose disease had progressed after first-line therapies.185 At a median follow-up of 18.4 months, median PFS and ORR for belzutifan 
were significantly favorable compared to everolimus (see Table 2). CR was observed in the interim analyses in the belzutifan arm but not in the 
everolimus arm. No statistically significant difference in OS was reported at a median follow-up of 25.7 months (see Table 2). The safety profile was 
similar to previous studies and incidence of grade 3–5 treatment-related AEs were similar between the two treatment arms.185 

Based on these data, the Panel included belzutifan as a category 2A, other recommended regimen for patients who had prior IO therapy, particularly 
those who received PD-1/L1 and VEGF inhibitors. For patients who are IO therapy naïve, belzutifan is a category 2B, useful in certain circumstances 
subsequent therapy option for patients with ccRCC. 

Lenvatinib + Pembrolizumab 
The phase II KEYNOTE-146 trial included three groups of patients: treatment-naïve; those who had previously received at least one line of treatment that 
did not include anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 ICIs; and those who had previously received at least one anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 ICI. See Table 2 for efficacy 
data. Treatment-naïve patients had the highest ORR and the longest PFS; ORR and PFS were comparable in the ICI-naïve and ICI treatment-
experienced groups. OS was longer only in the ICI-naïve group.186 In a longer follow-up, the ORR for treatment-naïve, previously treated but ICI-naïve, 

MS-24

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
and ICI-pretreated populations were consistent with previous observations (see Table 2). The median DOR was 24.2 months, 9 months, and 14.1 
months, respectively. The longer follow-up data showed OS and PFS benefit for lenvatinib + pembrolizumab in all three treatment groups with the 
treatment-naïve population showing the highest benefit, followed by ICI-pretreated groups, and then the pretreated ICI-naïve group.187 Hypertension, 
fatigue, and diarrhea were the most frequent treatment-related AEs and hypothyroidism was the most frequent immune-related AE.186 Based on these 
data, the Panel considers lenvatinib + pembrolizumab a category 2A, other recommended option for patients who are IO therapy naïve and a category 
2B, useful in certain circumstances option for patients with prior IO therapy. 

Tivozanib 
In March 2021, the FDA approved tivozanib, a multitargeted TKI of VEGFR-1, -2, and 3; c-KIT; and PDGFR-β for patients with relapsed or refractory 
advanced RCC who previously received two or more systemic therapies. Data from the randomized phase III TIVO-3 trial, which enrolled treatment-
experienced patients with relapsed or refractory advanced ccRCC, supported the drug’s approval. See Table 2 for efficacy data. Patients receiving 
tivozanib had significantly longer PFS than those receiving sorafenib; OS was similar between the two groups.188,189 In the extended follow-up, a 
statistically meaningful, higher 12-month landmark, PFS-conditioned OS was observed in those treated with tivozanib versus sorafenib, suggesting that 
some patients may have an OS benefit with tivozanib.189,190 Tivozanib also increased Q-TWiST as compared to sorafenib (15.04 months vs. 12.78 
months, respectively).191 Overall, incidence of AEs grade 3 or higher was lower in those treated with tivozanib compared to sorafenib. Common AEs 
grade 3 or higher were hypertension and asthenia.188,189 Additionally, tivozanib monotherapy was used as the control arm in the TiNivo-2 trial, as 
described previously, where there was no statistically significant PFS difference between the experimental and control arms in individuals who had 
received prior IO therapy.166 

Based on these data, the Panel considers tivozanib as a category 2A, other recommended subsequent therapy option for patients who have received 
prior IO therapy and a useful in certain circumstances option for those who are IO therapy naïve. 

Lenvatinib 
The Panel also includes lenvatinib as a subsequent therapy option useful in certain circumstances (category 2A) regardless of prior IO therapy status 
based on the phase II trial investigating everolimus/lenvatinib, lenvatinib monotherapy, and everolimus monotherapy described above.172,173 PFS favored 
lenvatinib monotherapy over everolimus monotherapy (see Table 2 for efficacy data). There was no statistically significant difference in OS between 
lenvatinib and everolimus monotherapy. No significant difference in PFS or OS was observed between lenvatinib monotherapy and the 
everolimus/lenvatinib combination.172,173 Common grade 3 treatment-emergent AEs in those who received lenvatinib monotherapy included proteinuria, 
hypertension, and diarrhea. Hypothyroidism was reported more frequently in those receiving single-agent lenvatinib or the combination compared to 
everolimus.172 

MS-25

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
Pazopanib 
A phase III trial comparing pazopanib with placebo, detailed earlier under the Other Recommended Regimens for first-line ccRCC, also included patients 
who had received prior cytokine therapy. PFS was significantly longer with pazopanib (7.4 months) versus placebo (4.2 months) in the treatment-
experienced sub-population (HR, 0.54; P < .001).151 However, OS was similar between the two groups (23 vs. 19 months, respectively; HR, 0.82).152 
Additionally, a prospective phase II trial evaluated second-line pazopanib in patients with advanced metastatic RCC previously treated with a targeted 
agent (ie, bevacizumab, sunitinib). Twenty-seven percent of patients had an OR to pazopanib; 49% had stable disease (SD). Median PFS was 7.5 
months, regardless of prior treatment regimen. Estimated OS rate at 24 months was 43%. AEs were mostly grade 1 or 2, and common grade 3 and 4 
AEs included diarrhea and hypertension, similar to the phase III study.192 Based on these data, the Panel considers pazopanib a category 2A, useful in 
certain circumstances subsequent therapy option for patients with ccRCC regardless of their prior IO therapy status. 

Sunitinib 
Sunitinib also has demonstrated substantial anti-tumor activity as a second-line therapy in patients with metastatic RCC who progressed on cytokine 
therapy.156,193 Sunitinib is considered a category 2A, useful in certain circumstances subsequent therapy option for patients with ccRCC regardless of 
their prior IO therapy status. 

Everolimus 
Everolimus (RAD001) is an orally administered mTOR inhibitor. In the randomized phase III RECORD-1 trial, everolimus was compared with placebo for 
the treatment of metastatic RCC in patients whose disease had progressed on treatment with sunitinib or sorafenib. The median PFS was significantly 
longer for everolimus versus placebo, but OS was similar between the two groups.194,195 Common AEs included stomatitis, fatigue, and rash, which 
generally were not severe. Pneumonitis of any grade was detected in <15% of patients treated with everolimus.194,195 Everolimus is listed as a category 
2A, useful in certain circumstances subsequent therapy option for patients with ccRCC regardless of their prior IO therapy status. 

Bevacizumab 
Phase II trials have shown benefit of bevacizumab monotherapy after prior treatment with a cytokine. In a phase II study investigating low- and high-dose 
bevacizumab versus placebo, bevacizumab extended time to progression of disease. Some patients receiving bevacizumab experienced hypertension or 
proteinuria, with no grade 4 or 5 AEs reported.196 Bevacizumab is a category 2B, useful in certain circumstances subsequent therapy option for patients 
with ccRCC regardless of their prior IO therapy status. 

Systemic Therapy for Patients with Stage IV (M1 or Unresectable T4,M0) or Relapsed Non-Clear Cell RCC 

Clinical trials of targeted agents have predominantly focused on patients with ccRCC due to the high prevalence of ccRCC.197 Data from systematic 
reviews, meta-analyses, and phase II studies with targeted agents also show some activity in patients with nccRCC. Compared with responses in 

MS-26

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
ccRCC, however, the response rates with these agents are significantly lower for nccRCC. Therefore, according to the Panel, enrollment in clinical trials 
is a preferred strategy for nccRCC and tumor genomic testing should be considered for trial eligibility. 

Non-Clear Cell RCC: Preferred 

Cabozantinib 
The randomized phase II SWOG 1500 trial compared the MET-targeted TKIs cabozantinib, crizotinib, and savolitinib with standard-of-care sunitinib in 
patients with advanced papillary RCC who had previously received up to 1 previous systemic therapy, excluding VEGF- and MET-targeted TKIs. 
Assignment to the crizotinib and savolitinib arms was halted due to results of a prespecified futility analysis. See Table 3 for efficacy data. Patients 
receiving cabozantinib had significantly longer PFS and a higher ORR than those receiving sunitinib.198 Final OS analysis did not show any significant 
difference in survival.199 The incidence of AEs grade 3 or 4 was highest for cabozantinib (74%), and the most common grade 3 or 4 AEs for cabozantinib 
were hypertension, fatigue, and hand-foot syndrome.198 Based on these data, the Panel included cabozantinib as a category 2A, preferred option for 
patients with nccRCC. 

Cabozantinib + Nivolumab 
Two separate patient cohorts defined by nccRCC histology in a phase II open-label trial received cabozantinib + nivolumab combination.200 ORR for 
patients with papillary, unclassified, or translocation RCC was 48% with a median follow-up time of 34 months. Median PFS was 13 months (95% CI, 7–
16) and median OS was 28 months (95% CI, 23–43).201 The most prevalent AEs of any grade were fatigue, diarrhea, and palmar-plantar 
erythrodysesthesia syndrome, and the most common grade 3 or 4 event was hypertension.200 Study of patients with chromophobe RCC closed early due 
to the lack of efficacy. Based on these results, the Panel added cabozantinib + nivolumab as a category 2A, preferred option for first or subsequent-line 
treatment of stage IV (M1 or unresectable T4,M0) or relapsed nccRCC. 

Lenvatinib + Pembrolizumab 
The phase II KEYNOTE-B61 trial investigated the combination of lenvatinib + pembrolizumab in untreated, advanced nccRCC.202,203 The primary 
endpoint was ORR, which was 49% in the initial analysis.202 A 22.8-month follow-up showed similar results (51% ORR).203 See Table 3 for all efficacy 
data. The most frequent treatment-related AEs of grade 3 or 4 included hypertension, stomatitis, and proteinuria.202 The Panel included lenvatinib + 
pembrolizumab as a category 2A, preferred option for patients in this setting. 

Non-Clear Cell RCC: Other Recommended 

Erlotinib + Bevacizumab for Advanced Papillary RCC, Including Hereditary Leiomyomatosis and Renal Cell Carcinoma Associated RCC 

Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma (HLRCC) is a hereditary condition in which affected patients are at risk for development of skin and 
uterine leiomyomas, as well as an aggressive form of papillary kidney cancer.204 

MS-27

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
In a phase II trial of patients with advanced papillary RCC (HLRCC-associated RCC; n = 43 or sporadic papillary RCC; n = 40), patients were treated 
with bevacizumab plus erlotinib.205 Some patients who were enrolled with either subtype received previous therapy (21% with HLRCC; 45% with sporadic 
papillary RCC), including a VEGFR TKI. The majority of patients had intermediate-risk disease. The ORR was 72% for those with HLRCC compared to 
35% with sporadic papillary RCC. Median PFS was 21.1 months in the HLRCC group compared to 8.9 months in the sporadic papillary RCC group. The 
most frequent AEs of grade 1–2 were acneiform rash, diarrhea, proteinuria, and dry skin, and of grade 3 or higher were hypertension and proteinuria.205 
Based on these data, the Panel recommends erlotinib + bevacizumab as a category 2A, other recommended option for select patients with nccRCC and 
papillary histology, including HLRCC. 

Everolimus/Lenvatinib 
Extrapolating on data from the phase III everolimus/lenvatinib trial in patients with ccRCC172 (see Subsequent Systemic Therapy Options for Patients with 
ccRCC), the Panel added the combination therapy as a category 2A, other recommended regimen for patients with nccRCC. 

They also reviewed data206 from a single-arm phase II trial (ie, NCT02915783) that enrolled patients with unresectable advanced or metastatic nccRCC 
who had not previously received prior systemic therapy. All patients in the trial received combination everolimus/lenvatinib. See Table 3 for efficacy data. 
Authors reported that ORR was 26% (95% CI, 12–45). Eight patients in the trial achieved a PR (papillary, n = 3; chromophobe, n = 4; unclassified, n = 1); 
no patients had a CR. The median DOR was NE. Eighteen patients (58.1%) had SD, and the clinical benefit rate (CR + PR + durable SD [duration ≥23 
weeks]) was 61% (95% CI, 42–78). The median PFS was 9.2 months (95% CI, 5.5–NE) and OS was 15.6 months (95% CI, 9.2–NE). AEs of any grade 
that occurred in >50% of patients included fatigue, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite.206 While the Panel conceded that the number of 
enrolled patients was small, they generally felt that everolimus/lenvatinib treatment led to improved patient outcomes across all nccRCC subtypes. 

Nivolumab 
A retrospective analysis evaluated the response to at least one dose of nivolumab in patients with metastatic nccRCC.207 See Table 3 for efficacy data. 
This study evaluated 35 patients for response and found that 20% had a PR and 29% had SD, with a median follow-up of 8.5 months and median PFS of 
3.5 months. Fatigue, fever, rash, and hypothyroidism were the most common AEs observed. A separate retrospective analysis found modest responses 
with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in 43 patients also with metastatic nccRCC.208 An OR was achieved in eight patients (19%), including four patients (13%) who 
received PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy. Based on these data, the Panel considers nivolumab a category 2A, other recommended regimen for patients with 
nccRCC. 

Pembrolizumab 
Cohort B of the phase II KEYNOTE-427 study assessed the efficacy and safety of pembrolizumab monotherapy in 165 patients with systemic therapy-
naïve, newly diagnosed or recurrent stage IV nccRCC.209 See Table 3 for efficacy data. The majority (about 72%) of patients had confirmed papillary 
RCC, about 13% had chromophobe RCC, and about 16% had unclassified RCC histology. ORR across all subtypes was approximately 27% (ORR by 
histology was 29% for papillary, 10% for chromophobe, and 31% for unclassified). Overall PFS and OS were 4.2 months and 28.9 months, respectively. 

MS-28

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
Treatment-related AEs of any grade experienced by patients were most commonly pruritus, fatigue, hypothyroidism, and diarrhea.209 Based on these 
data, the Panel added pembrolizumab as a category 2A, other recommended regimen for patients with nccRCC. 

Sunitinib 
Two randomized phase II studies compared first-line sunitinib with first-line everolimus in patients with nccRCC. See Table 3 for efficacy data. While data 
from the ASPEN trial210 suggested that patients receiving sunitinib had significantly longer PFS than those receiving everolimus, data from the ESPN 
trial211 suggested that both OS and PFS were similar between the two groups. Common AEs of grade 3 or 4 observed in both trials included 
hypertension, diarrhea, and fatigue. Other AEs of grade 3 or 4 in the ESPN trial that were of lower incidence in the ASPEN trial included neutropenia and 
anemia.210,211 

Additionally, a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials for patients with nccRCC found that TKI treatment reduced the risk of progression compared 
with mTOR inhibitors.212 The study found that sunitinib significantly reduced the risk of progression compared to everolimus in the first-line setting. 
However, no significant differences between TKIs and mTOR inhibitor treatment were found for OS and ORR. 

Based on these data and the phase II SWOG 1500 trial results,198 the Panel decided sunitinib is a category 2A, other recommended option for patients 
with nccRCC. 

Non-Clear Cell RCC: Useful in Certain Circumstances 

Axitinib 
A phase II trial of axitinib in 40 patients with recurrent or metastatic nccRCC that progressed after treatment with temsirolimus found a median PFS of 7.4 
months, median OS of 12.1 months, and ORR of 37.5%. The most common AEs were hypertension, anorexia, cough, and plantar erythrodysesthesia, 
which were mostly low grade.213 The Panel considers axitinib a category 2A, useful in certain circumstances option for patients with nccRCC. 

Everolimus 
The efficacy and safety of everolimus in patients with metastatic nccRCC were evaluated in a subgroup of 75 patients enrolled in the REACT trial. ORR 
and rate of SD were similar between patients with ccRCC and nccRCC.214 In a phase II study of treatment-experienced patients with nccRCC,215 median 
OS was 14 months, ORR was 10.2%, and median PFS was 5.2 months. About 47% of patients experienced AEs of grade 3 or higher, which included 
anemia and hyperglycemia.215 According to data from the phase II RAPTOR trial,216 median OS ranged from 24 to 28 months and median PFS ranged 
from 5 to 8 months, depending on type of papillary nccRCC; patients with type 1 nccRCC had better responses than those with type 2 histology. The 
most common AEs of any grade in >30% of patients were rash, cough, asthenia, mucosal inflammation, diarrhea, and decreased appetite.216 Based on 
these data, the Panel included everolimus as a category 2A, useful in certain circumstances option for patients with nccRCC. 

MS-29

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
Everolimus + Bevacizumab 
A phase II trial of 34 treatment-naïve patients with metastatic nccRCC studied the efficacy and safety of treatment with bevacizumab plus everolimus.217 
Median PFS, OS, and ORR were 11.0 months, 18.5 months, and 29%, respectively. Patients with tumors that contained appreciable papillary or 
chromophobe elements showed significantly higher PFS and ORR than other histologies. Most AEs were grade 1 or 2, and AEs of grade 3 or 4 included 
hypertension, proteinuria, lymphopenia, hyperglycemia, and hypertriglyceridemia.217 Based on these data, the Panel recommends everolimus + 
bevacizumab as a category 2A, useful in certain circumstances option for patients with nccRCC. 

Ipilimumab + Nivolumab 
A cohort of 52 patients with advanced nccRCC of the phase 3/4 Checkmate 920 trial received four doses of ipilimumab/nivolumab combination followed 
by nivolumab for ≤2 years or until disease progression. With 24.1 months of minimum study follow-up, the ORR was 19.6% with a median PFS of 3.7 
months and median OS of 21.2 months (95% CI, 16.6–NE).218 The most common AEs of any grade were rash, diarrhea/colitis, and 
hypothyroidism/thyroiditis. Reported AEs of grade 3 or 4 included diarrhea/colitis, rash, nephritis/renal dysfunction, adrenal insufficiency, hepatitis, and 
hypophysitis. 

The randomized phase II SUNNIFORECAST trial investigated ipilimumab/nivolumab in patients with untreated, advanced nccRCC.219 Patients were 
randomized to either ipilimumab/nivolumab (n = 157) or investigator’s choice of a standard approved regimen (n = 152). OS rate at 12 months was 78% 
(95% CI, 71–84) with ipilimumab/nivolumab versus 68% (95% CI, 60–75) with standard of care (P = .026).219 Median OS, PFS, and ORR with 
ipilimumab/nivolumab were 33.2 months, 5.4 months, and 33%, respectively. The same measures with standard-of-care therapy were 25.2 months, 5.7 
months, and 20%, respectively. Results were similar in subgroup analyses by histology (ie, papillary and non-papillary RCC). Incidence of AEs (any 
grade or serious AEs) were similar between treatment arms.219 

Based on these data, the Panel includes ipilimumab + nivolumab as a category 2B option, useful in certain circumstances for advanced nccRCC. 

Additional Treatment Options for Rare Types of nccRCC 
Among the nccRCC histologies, renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) is extremely rare, comprising approximately 2% of all primary renal tumors in young 
people.220,221 Metastatic disease is seen at presentation in 67% to 95% of patients.220-222 Chemotherapy remains the focus of treatment for this subtype, 
although the prognosis remains dismal. 

Collecting-duct carcinoma is also a very rare type of nccRCC, often presenting at an advanced stage of disease. Up to 40% of patients have metastatic 
spread at initial presentation, and most patients die within 1 to 3 years from the time of primary diagnosis.223-226 Collecting duct carcinoma shares biologic 
features with urothelial carcinoma. In a multicenter prospective study, 23 patients with no prior therapy were treated with a combination of gemcitabine 
and either cisplatin or carboplatin.227 The results showed a response rate of 26% and an OS of 10.5 months.227 

MS-30

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
The Panel notes that in patients with other nccRCC subtypes such as collecting duct or medullary subtypes, PRs to cytotoxic chemotherapy have been 
observed (gemcitabine in combination with carboplatin or cisplatin; or paclitaxel with carboplatin) as well as for other platinum-based chemotherapies 
currently used for urothelial carcinomas. Gemcitabine in combination with doxorubicin can also produce responses in patients with RMC.222,228,229 Oral 
targeted therapies generally do not produce responses in patients with RMC. Erlotinib in combination with bevacizumab can produce responses even in 
heavily pretreated patients with RMC. Outside of clinical trials, platinum-based chemotherapy regimens should be the preferred first-line therapy for 
RMC. 

Follow-up Recommendations for Relapsed or Stage IV Disease and Surgically Unresectable Disease 

The Panel recommends an H&P examination of patients every 6 to 16 weeks for patients receiving systemic therapy, or more frequently as clinically 
indicated. Other laboratory evaluations may be carried out as per the requirements for the therapeutic agent being used. 

Imaging tests such as CT or MRI (both with and without IV contrast unless contraindicated) should be performed prior to initiating systemic 
treatment/observation; subsequent imaging may be performed every 6 to 16 weeks as per the physician’s discretion, patient’s clinical status, and 
therapeutic schedule. Imaging interval frequency should be altered according to rate of disease change and sites of active disease. MRI (preferred) or 
CT of head at baseline can be considered, as clinically indicated. Annual surveillance scans can be performed at the physician’s discretion. The Panel 
recommends additional imaging such as MRI of spine and bone scan as clinically indicated. As is recommended with follow-up for stage III and 
resectable stage IV disease, the Panel recommends FDG-PET be used during follow-up if a patient has FH-deficient or SDHB-deficient RCC.37 Another 
study investigated the use of FDG-PET for detection of bone metastases in 18 patients with RCC and found that FDG-PET was more accurate and 
sensitive in detecting bone metastases in these patients than bone scan.38 FDG-PET is also recommended if a patient has bone-predominant disease or 
if evaluation takes place prior to metastasectomy. 

Supportive Care 

Supportive care remains a mainstay of therapy for all patients with metastatic RCC (see NCCN Guidelines for Palliative Care available at 
www.NCCN.org). The Panel recommends radiation therapy as a supportive care option, where SBRT is the preferred approach. SBRT can be used for 
palliative treatment of symptomatic extracranial metastases.230-232 See Principles of Radiation Therapy in these Guidelines for specific recommendations. 

Brain metastasis occurs in ~2% to 8% of patients with advanced RCC, depending on histologic type of RCC.233 Surgery may be an option for certain 
patients with oligometastatic disease in the brain whose disease is well-controlled extracranially. Whole brain radiation should only be considered for 
palliative care in patients with good performance status and disease progression where stereotactic radiosurgery and fractionated stereotactic radiation 
are not feasible. Pros and cons should be weighed based on patient goals.234 For recommendations and dosing regimens for brain metastases, as well 
as whole brain radiation regimens, see Principles of Radiation Therapy in the Guidelines. 

MS-31

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
Surgery also may be appropriate for selected patients with malignant spinal cord compression or impending or actual fractures in weight-bearing bones. 
The frequency of clinic visits or radiographic and laboratory assessments depends on the individual needs of the patient. 

Bone metastasis occurs in ~30% to 40% of patients with advanced RCC.14,233,235 Bone lesions in patients with RCC are typically osteolytic and cause 
considerable morbidity, leading to skeletal-related events (SREs), including bone pain with need for surgery or radiotherapy, hypercalcemia, pathologic 
fractures, and spinal cord compression. Two studies of patients with bone metastases showed an improvement in bone pain using different radiotherapy 
modalities.236,237 

The role of bone-modifying agents such as bisphosphonates (eg, zoledronic acid) has been established in patients with various malignancies.238,239 The 
bone-modifying agent approved for use in patients with RCC that has metastasized to the bone is the RANK-L inhibitor, denosumab. A phase III 
randomized trial directly compared the development of SREs on either denosumab or zoledronic acid in patients with multiple myeloma or bone 
metastases with a solid tumor (excluding breast or prostate cancer).240 The study enrolled 1597 patients with solid tumors, including patients with RCC (n 
= 155). Time to first on-study SRE was 21.4 months with denosumab in patients with solid tumors compared to 15.4 months with zoledronic acid (HR, 
0.81; 95% CI, 0.68–0.96; P = .017).241 

The Panel accepts the use of a bisphosphonate or a RANK ligand inhibitor in select cases for a patient with bony metastases and creatinine clearance 
≥30 mL/min. Calcium and vitamin D daily supplements are highly recommended with use of these agents.240 An FDA-approved biosimilar is an 
appropriate substitute for denosumab. Treatment for the palliation of symptoms, especially in patients with marginal performance status and evidence of 
metastatic disease, includes optimal pain management (see NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain, available at www.NCCN.org). 

Hereditary RCC Syndromes 

While hereditary RCC is relatively rare (around 3% of all RCC cases),242 the Panel felt that it was important to provide recommendations for patients with 
a suspected or confirmed hereditary RCC syndrome. Accordingly, the Guidelines now describe seven of the most common hereditary RCC syndromes 
that may predispose patients to RCC: BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome (BAP1-TPDS), Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome (BHDS), HLRCC (FH-deficient), 
hereditary papillary renal carcinoma (HPRC), hereditary paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome (SDH-deficient), tuberous sclerosis 
complex (TSC), and VHL disease. The Guidelines describe kidney-specific clinical features and manifestations of each of these syndromes and known 
associated genes/inheritance patterns. They also provide genetic testing, surveillance, and treatment recommendations for individuals who are 
suspected or confirmed to have a hereditary RCC syndrome. While published data informed the majority of these recommendations, the Panel also 
relied on the real-world experience and expertise of the hereditary subcommittee members to develop recommendations in instances of limited data. 

The subcommittee notes that there are some syndromes associated with RCC that overlap with other cancers (eg, Cowden syndrome, Lynch syndrome). 
For Cowden and Lynch syndromes, the Panel refers readers to the information provided in the NCCN Guidelines for Genetic/Familial High-Risk 
Assessment: Breast, Ovarian, Pancreatic, and Prostate (available at www.NCCN.org). Future versions of the Guidelines may be expanded to include 

MS-32

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
other hereditary syndromes such as microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF)-associated cancer syndrome, which predisposes patients to 
melanoma and/or RCC.25 

The subcommittee also notes that patients with hereditary RCC syndromes often experience non-renal manifestations but felt that input from clinicians 
from other specialties (eg, dermatology, endocrinology, neurology, ophthalmology, urology) would be necessary to provide consensus-based 
recommendations for all potential manifestations. Accordingly, the scope is currently limited to kidney-specific clinical features and manifestations, but 
the subcommittee identified specialists who may be helpful in managing non-renal manifestations in patients with a hereditary RCC syndrome. 
Recommendations for genetic testing, surveillance, and treatment vary according to the individual’s personal and/or family history of a hereditary RCC 
syndrome or clinical diagnosis of RCC. Below is a summary of recommendations by patient population. 

Genetic Testing and Surveillance Recommendations for Individuals with a Personal or Family History of an RCC Syndrome 

The Panel recommends that individuals with a personal or family history of an RCC syndrome or individuals with syndrome features should undergo 
genetic evaluation. For criteria to be met for further genetic risk evaluation for hereditary RCC syndromes and their histologies, inheritance patterns, and 
clinical manifestations, see HERED-RCC-1 and HERED-RCC-2 in the algorithm. If patients harbor a familial pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic 
mutation associated with an RCC syndrome, they should undergo screening for the development of RCC. 

For kidney-specific screening in patients who are confirmed to have a hereditary RCC syndrome, but who do not yet have a radiographic or pathologic 
diagnosis of RCC, the Panel recommends use of abdomen MRI (preferred). CT may also be used for surgical planning purposes, but the Panel warns 
that use of abdomen CT should be limited due to the potential of increased lifetime radiation exposure. The Panel also includes recommendations on 
testing intervals and the age at which patients should begin regular screening, as both vary widely by the hereditary RCC syndrome in question. While 
patients with HLRCC should undergo imaging annually,204 those with less aggressive syndromes such as TSC may benefit from testing at longer 
intervals.243-246 

The age at which patients should begin screening also varies by hereditary RCC syndrome. The Panel recommends that patients with confirmed 
HLRCC, PGL/PCC, TSC, and VHL disease should begin screening in childhood.204,243-247 In contrast, those with BAP1-TPDS, BHDS, or HPRC should 
begin screening in adulthood (ie, age 20 years for BHDS, age 30 years for BAP1-TPDS and HPRC).243,248,249 ,250 However, the Panel notes that if a 
patient has a known family member with an early diagnosis of hereditary RCC, screening should begin 10 years before the age that the family member 
was diagnosed, regardless of the syndrome in question. 

Genetic Testing and Screening Recommendations for Patients with a Clinical Diagnosis of RCC Who Have Characteristics Consistent with 
Inherited RCC 

The Panel includes recommendations for patients who already have a clinical or pathologic diagnosis of RCC and have characteristics potentially 
associated with a hereditary syndrome. This includes RCC diagnosis at ≤46 years of age (though not as sensitive when used as a single criterion), 

MS-33

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
presence of bilateral or multifocal tumors, ≥1 known first- or second-degree relative with RCC, and/or a personal or family history of mesothelioma or 
uveal melanoma. These patients should also undergo genetic risk assessment, and if indicated, genetic testing. The Panel also recommends genetic risk 
evaluation for hereditary RCC syndromes for unaffected individuals who have ≥2 first- or second-degree relatives with RCC (on the same side of the 
family) and/or any first-degree relative with clinical or pathologic diagnosis of a hereditary RCC syndrome who is unable or unwilling to genetically test. If 
inherited RCC is confirmed, patients should undergo screening as described above, in addition to disease stage-appropriate surveillance. 

Kidney-Specific Surgical Recommendations for Patients with a Confirmed Hereditary RCC Syndrome 

The Panel also provides surgical recommendations for the majority of the included hereditary RCC syndromes, which are based on published data 
and/or the subcommittee’s real-world experience in treating patients with these syndromes. In order to develop these recommendations, they carefully 
weighed the potential morbidity and mortality of surgical treatment against the potential aggressiveness of each of the syndromes. They agreed that 
patients with BHDS, HPRC, and TSC may benefit from more conservative treatment, such as nephron-sparing surgery or percutaneous ablation,251,252 
while patients with HLRCC/FH-deficient RCC should undergo total radical nephrectomy.204 The Panel’s recommendations for surgical treatment of 
PGL/PCC/SDH-deficient RCC vary by tumor size and histology: those with smaller, less aggressive tumors may be eligible for partial nephrectomy, while 
those with larger, more aggressive tumors (eg, high-grade, sarcomatoid) should undergo radical nephrectomy.253 For both HLRCC/FH-deficient RCC and 
PGL/PCC/SDH-deficient RCC, the Panel indicates that FDG-PET is useful for staging pre-nephrectomy, as well as for surveillance.37,38 Tumor size also 
factored into the Panel’s surgical recommendations for patients with VHL disease; they noted that these patients are likely to undergo multiple surgical 
resections during their lifetime that may contribute to chronic and progressive renal failure. Thus, the timing of surgical intervention must be carefully 
determined to limit the development of metastases and morbidity associated with surgical intervention. They agreed that only patients with VHL disease 
with tumors approaching 3 cm in diameter should undergo partial nephrectomy (or percutaneous ablation if nephrectomy is contraindicated).252,254 

Kidney-Specific Systemic Therapy for Patients with Confirmed Hereditary RCC 

The Guidelines include a limited number of kidney-specific systemic therapy recommendations for patients with hereditary RCC. 

Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) Angiomyolipoma 
Everolimus was approved in April 2012 for treating TSC-associated benign renal angiomyolipomas not requiring immediate surgery based on the 
randomized phase III EXIST-2 trial.255 In the 4-year update, results were reported for both patients who were originally randomized to everolimus and 
those who later received everolimus in an unblinded extension phase (n = 112). Confirmed angiomyolipoma response was reported in 58% of patients, 
and ≥75% had a persistent angiomyolipoma volume decrease of at least 30%.256 The Panel included everolimus as a category 2A, preferred 
recommendation for patients with TSC-associated angiomyolipoma. 

The Panel also included sirolimus as an option in this setting (category 2A, other recommended). Sirolimus, another mTOR inhibitor, was investigated for 
the treatment of patients with TSC or sporadic lymphangioleiomyomatosis in a phase I/II trial.257 At the 12-month mark, angiomyolipoma volume (primary 

MS-34

pages.title: Kidney Cancer
pages.text:
endpoint) was reduced by ≥30% for 16 out of 20 patients assessed. Angiomyolipoma volume was also evaluated a year after ending sirolimus treatment, 
and 5 out of 18 evaluable patients continued to show a volume reduction (≥30%). Common AEs included gastrointestinal events and upper respiratory 
infections.257 

Hereditary Leiomyomatosis and Renal Cell Cancer (HLRCC) 
The Panel included erlotinib + bevacizumab for patients with HLRCC/FH-deficient-associated metastatic RCC. While this regimen is not FDA-approved 
for use in this patient population, its inclusion is supported by clinical trial data showing improved patient outcomes. A phase II study investigating 
erlotinib + bevacizumab treatment in patients with HLRCC (n = 43) or sporadic papillary RCC (n = 40) was described above (see Non-Clear Cell RCC: 
Other Recommended and Table 3 for detailed information). As described above, erlotinib + bevacizumab treatment led to a 72% ORR in patients with 
HLRCC-associated RCC, median PFS of 21.1 months, and median DOR of 19.3 months.205 Based on these data, the Panel considers erlotinib + 
bevacizumab a category 2A, other recommended option for patients with HLRCC-associated RCC. 

Though data are limited for cabozantinib + nivolumab in HLRCC-associated RCC, the Panel felt that for certain patients this combination can be an 
option (useful in certain circumstances, category 2A). In the phase II trial investigating cabozantinib + nivolumab in nccRCC discussed earlier, a small 
subset of patients had FH-deficient RCC (n = 5). Though the sample size was small, the authors noted that an OR was observed in these five patients.200 

von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) Disease 
In August 2021, the FDA approved belzutifan for the treatment of patients with VHL disease-associated RCC who require therapy for RCC but do not 
require immediate surgery. LITESPARK-004, an open-label, phase II clinical trial, enrolled 61 patients with VHL-associated RCC; 97% had previously 
undergone a tumor reduction procedure.258 The major efficacy endpoint was ORR, which was 49% (95% CI, 36–62) after a median follow-up of 21.8 
months, with 30 patients confirming PRs. Updated results from a 50-month follow-up reported an ORR of 67%, with a CR observed in seven patients and 
a PR in 34 patients.259 SD was identified in another 30 patients (49%). Median time to response was 8.2 months and median DOR was not reached.258 
The Panel considers belzutifan a category 2A, preferred option for patients with VHL-associated-RCC. 

The Panel also considers pazopanib a category 2A, useful in certain circumstances option for patients with VHL disease-associated nonmetastatic 
lesions. In a phase II trial, pazopanib led to a 42% ORR and a 52% renal tumor-specific response rate in 31 patients with VHL disease.260 

Data Summary 

The following tables summarize the key data supporting the inclusion of systemic therapy category 1 and 2A, preferred, and other recommended 
treatment options for ccRCC and nccRCC. Table 1 includes data on recommended first-line systemic therapies for patients with ccRCC. Table 2 includes 
data on recommended subsequent systemic therapies for patients with ccRCC. Table 3 includes data on recommended systemic therapies for patients 
with nccRCC. For all tables, the most recent data are reported unless otherwise indicated.

suspicious_renal_mass.definition: True if imaging or clinical assessment describes a suspicious renal mass (the entry point for the kidney workup).

histology.definition: Histologic subtype of the renal tumor: clear_cell, or non_clear_cell (any non-clear cell histology), or other (histology not stated or not classifiable).

clinical_t_category.definition: Clinical primary tumor (T) category as stated in the case. other = not stated or not in this list.

n_category.definition: Clinical regional lymph node (N) category as stated in the case. other = not stated or not in this list.

m_category.definition: Clinical distant metastasis (M) category as stated in the case. other = not stated or not in this list.

primary_resectability.definition: Clinician's assessment of whether the primary tumor can be surgically removed, as recorded in the case: resectable, potentially_resectable (potentially surgically resectable), or unresectable. other = not recorded.

syndrome_features_present.definition: True if the individual has clinical features of a hereditary kidney cancer syndrome (HERED-RCC-2) as stated in the case.

meets_hereditary_rcc1_criteria.definition: Clinician judgement that the individual meets the criteria in HERED-RCC-1 for hereditary kidney cancer risk evaluation.

familial_plp_variant_known.definition: True if a familial pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) germline variant is known in the family; false if no familial P/LP variant is known.

germline_test_result.definition: Result of germline genetic testing as stated in the case: plp_variant_found (pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant), no_plp_variant_found, vus_found_uninformative (variant of uncertain significance), not_tested, or other.

hereditary_rcc_pathway.definition: True if the individual has syndrome features (HERED-RCC-2) or meets the HERED-RCC-1 criteria.

stage_group.definition: Clinical stage group from T, N and M categories. Most specific or highest category first.

notes.predicates: Conditions were drafted and reviewed by a language model (model_reviewed), not by clinicians. 'rejected' means the review rejected the draft; the box then needs clinician judgement. 'section_only' means the box only requires the patient to be in the page's guideline section.
notes.coordinates: bbox and line_bboxes are PDF points with the origin at the page's top left; pages[].size gives the page size.
notes.links: page links name a page id from pages[]; a multi-page code such as PROS-F has ids 'PROS-F 1 of 5' ... ; external_guideline links name another guideline's slug.
